title: The Time Machine
description: H. G. Wells's 1895 novella: a Victorian inventor travels to the year 802,701 and finds humanity split into two species, the gentle Eloi above ground and the Morlocks below, then rides on to the dying sun.

cover.alt: The White Sphinx in the garden of the year 802,701
cover.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Keep the rich in the sun and the workers underground long enough, and they stop being two classes. They become two species, and one eats the other.

images.alt: Underground, the Time Traveller holds off the Morlocks with a match
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The future is not ruined by disaster but by success: a humanity with nothing left to struggle against forgets how to think.

images.alt: The Eloi garland the Time Traveller with flowers
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Wells shows the end of the species and the death of the sun, and leaves the reader holding two small dried flowers.

images.alt: Two strange white flowers, Weena's gift
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Ten years before Einstein's special relativity, the Time Traveller explains his idea after dinner to sceptical guests.
chunks.source_quote: There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it.

images.alt: The Time Traveller's guests watch the model machine vanish
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: His first theory of the future is a pastoral one: the Eloi are what people become when all problems have been solved.
chunks.source_quote: The ruddy sunset set me thinking of the sunset of mankind.

images.alt: The White Sphinx in the garden of the year 802,701
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The second theory is Victorian economics run forward: the workers driven underground, the owners left with the surface.
chunks.source_quote: above ground you must have the Haves, pursuing pleasure and comfort and beauty, and below ground the Have-nots

images.alt: The wells that lead down to the Morlocks
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The final theory is the horror of the book: the masters have become livestock and the servants farm them.
chunks.source_quote: These Eloi were mere fatted cattle, which the ant-like Morlocks preserved and preyed upon

images.alt: The fire in the forest, where Weena is lost
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The Traveller's moral is biological, not political: intelligence exists to solve problems, and fades when the problems go.
chunks.source_quote: It is a law of nature we overlook, that intellectual versatility is the compensation for change, danger, and trouble.

images.alt: The Palace of Green Porcelain, a ruined museum
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Rip Van Winkle travels twenty years into the future by sleeping, the Time Traveller eight hundred thousand by machine. Both come back to a room of people who half believe them, and both are changed into storytellers whose evidence is thin: Rip has a rusty gun, the Traveller two strange flowers.

images.alt: Travelling: days flicker past and the sun streaks across the sky
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: In Shards: Echo, a pilot flees far enough to hear the broadcasts of a humanity that no longer exists. On the terminal beach the Time Traveller goes further still: thirty million years on, under a swollen red sun, he is the only human witness to the end. Both stories use distance in space or time to let one person see the whole species from outside.

images.alt: The terminal beach under the dying red sun
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Wells trained as a biologist under T. H. Huxley, Darwin's great defender, at the Normal School of Science in South Kensington. The Time Machine, his first novel, grew from articles on time travel he wrote as a student and appeared as a book in 1895. Its dying sun reflects the physics of the day, in which Lord Kelvin had argued that the sun was slowly cooling.

images.alt: The Time Traveller returns, dishevelled, to dinner
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text:
The Time Machine took the idea of evolution, which Victorians often heard as a promise of progress, and showed that it promises nothing. Natural selection only fits creatures to their conditions, and if those conditions are easy, the fit creature is soft and stupid. The Eloi are not punished; they are perfectly adapted. Wells turns this into a parable of class: a leisure class that no longer works and a working class that no longer sees the sun, until the relationship between them reverses.

The book is also the first story to treat time as a place you can drive to, and almost every later time-travel story borrows its machine. But its most haunting chapter goes beyond the Eloi to a beach where the last life on Earth is crabs and lichen under a dying red sun. Against that scale the Traveller's small loyalty to Weena, the Eloi woman who followed him, is the book's counterweight. The narrator, who never sees the Traveller again, chooses to keep the flowers rather than the despair.

images.alt: The Eloi garland the Time Traveller with flowers
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.
